title: Water
tagline: The universal solvent — solutions, hydration, hardness, softening and the drying agents that remove water.

sourceNote.boardprep: Original study material written by BoardPrep for the CISCE ICSE Class IX Chemistry syllabus (official-verified baseline, examination year 2027). No board examination paper was consulted, so every question is original practice and not a previous year question.

overview.intro: Water is the commonest solvent in the laboratory and the solvent of life, and its properties explain a great deal of everyday chemistry. This chapter treats water as a solvent (solutions, saturated solutions and concentration), as a component of crystals (hydrated substances and water of crystallisation), and as a contaminant in supply (hardness, its causes, its consequences and its removal). You will also meet the drying agents used to keep gases and liquids dry, and learn which drying agent is safe for which substance — a favourite source of exam errors.

facts.label: Hardness causes
facts.value: Dissolved hydrogen carbonates of calcium and magnesium (temporary); sulphates and chlorides of calcium and magnesium (permanent)

facts.label: Test for water
facts.value: Anhydrous copper(II) sulphate turns from white to blue

facts.label: Water of crystallisation
facts.value: Fixed number of water molecules held in a crystal lattice, e.g. CuSO4.5H2O

learn.title: Water as a solvent: solutions and concentration

blocks.text: A solution is a homogeneous mixture of a solute dissolved in a solvent. Water dissolves more substances than any other common liquid — hence its title of universal solvent — because its polar molecules surround and stabilise ions and polar molecules. A solution that holds the maximum solute at a given temperature is saturated; adding more solute then leaves undissolved solid in equilibrium with the solution. Solutions are described as dilute (little solute per unit solvent) or concentrated (much solute), and concentration can be expressed as mass of solute per volume of solution or as grams of solute per 100 cm3 of solvent.

items.meaning: A homogeneous mixture of one or more solutes in a solvent, with particles too small to scatter light or settle.
The substance that dissolves, such as sodium chloride in salt water.
A solution that contains the maximum amount of solute dissolved at that temperature, in equilibrium with undissolved solute.
A heterogeneous mixture whose particles are large enough to settle and scatter light, such as muddy water.
A mixture with intermediate particle size — particles do not settle but scatter light, such as milk or starch solution.

items: Solutions are clear and do not scatter a light beam (no Tyndall effect); suspensions settle on standing; colloids scatter light but do not settle.
Filtration separates an insoluble solid from a liquid; evaporation separates a dissolved solid from its solvent.
Concentration calculations use: mass of solute = (concentration / 100) x mass or volume of solution.
Increasing temperature usually increases solubility for solids; for gases, increasing temperature decreases solubility.

items.text: Dissolving 10 g of a salt in 90 g of water gives 100 g of solution that is 10 per cent by mass.
items.note: Percent by mass uses the mass of the whole solution in the denominator, not the mass of the solvent.

items.text: Filtering chalk dust from water leaves the chalk on the paper; the filtrate is water.
items.note: Chalk is insoluble, so filtration works; sodium chloride would pass through with the water.

learn.title: Hydrated substances and water of crystallisation

blocks.text: Many crystals trap a fixed number of water molecules inside their lattice; this is water of crystallisation and such crystals are called hydrated. The water is held in fixed proportion, so heating drives it off and leaves the anhydrous form — for example blue copper(II) sulphate crystals (CuSO4.5H2O) become white anhydrous copper(II) sulphate (CuSO4) on strong heating. Adding water to the anhydrous solid restores the blue colour and releases heat; this reversible change is the standard laboratory test for water. Substances that have lost their water of crystallisation may still dissolve, but they often differ in appearance and properties from the hydrated form.

items: Copper(II) sulphate pentahydrate CuSO4.5H2O — blue vitriol; anhydrous form is white.
Washing soda Na2CO3.10H2O — efflorescent; it loses water in dry air.
Gypsum is CaSO4.2H2O; carefully heating gypsum gives plaster of paris, written (CaSO4)2.H2O — two CaSO4 units sharing one water molecule.
The dot in the formula does not mean multiplication — it means the molecules are held in the lattice.
Water of crystallisation is fixed for a compound: CuSO4 always carries five water molecules when fully hydrated.

items.text: Test for water: add a few drops to white anhydrous copper(II) sulphate — it turns blue.
items.note: CuSO4 (white) + 5H2O -> CuSO4.5H2O (blue); the colour change confirms water.
Each formula unit of gypsum loses one and a half water molecules: careful heating removes water without driving off the water the hemihydrate still holds, or the plaster will not set.
Water vapour condenses on the cooler part of the test tube — visible evidence of water of crystallisation.

items.meaning: A crystalline solid containing a fixed number of water molecules in its lattice, such as CuSO4.5H2O.
A substance containing no water of crystallisation, such as white CuSO4.
Water molecules held in fixed proportion within a crystal lattice.
Loss of water of crystallisation to dry air, leaving a powdery anhydrous surface.

learn.title: Hardness of water and its removal

blocks.text: Pure water lathers freely with soap; hard water does not. Hardness is caused by dissolved calcium and magnesium salts. Temporary hardness is due to hydrogen carbonates such as Ca(HCO3)2, which decompose on boiling and are therefore removed by boiling: Ca(HCO3)2 ->(heat) CaCO3 + H2O + CO2. Permanent hardness is due to sulphates and chlorides such as CaSO4 and MgCl2, which are unaffected by boiling and need other methods. Softening methods include boiling (temporary only), adding washing soda (precipitates the calcium and magnesium salts), ion-exchange columns (replace Ca2+ and Mg2+ with Na+) and distillation (removes all dissolved solids, giving pure water).

items: Hard water wastes soap: it forms a scum (calcium or magnesium stearate) instead of lather.
Scale in kettles and boilers is calcium carbonate and calcium sulphate deposited from hard water — it wastes fuel and can block pipes.
Boiling removes temporary hardness only; permanent hardness survives boiling.
Washing soda Na2CO3.10H2O softens both types by precipitating insoluble carbonates.
Distillation gives the purest water and removes both temporary and permanent hardness.

items.text: Temporary hardness removed by boiling: Ca(HCO3)2 ->(heat) CaCO3(s) + H2O + CO2(g).
items.note: The insoluble calcium carbonate is the white scale left in the kettle.

items.text: Softening with washing soda: CaSO4(aq) + Na2CO3(aq) -> CaCO3(s) + Na2SO4(aq).
items.note: Carbonate ions precipitate calcium as insoluble calcium carbonate, replacing it with soluble sodium salts.

items.text: Soap reaction in hard water: 2C17H35COONa + CaCl2 -> (C17H35COO)2Ca (scum) + 2NaCl.
items.note: The insoluble calcium salt of the fatty acid is the scum — soap molecules are lost to it instead of forming lather.

items.meaning: Hardness caused by hydrogen carbonates of calcium and magnesium; removable by boiling.
Hardness caused by sulphates and chlorides of calcium and magnesium; not removed by boiling.
Insoluble precipitate formed when soap reacts with calcium or magnesium ions in hard water.
Hard deposit of calcium carbonate/sulphate formed on heated surfaces by hard water.
Boiling followed by condensation, giving pure water free of all dissolved solids.

blocks.text: A drying agent (desiccant) removes water vapour from a substance without reacting with it. Common laboratory drying agents are anhydrous calcium chloride, concentrated sulphuric acid, phosphorus(V) oxide and quicklime (calcium oxide). The choice depends on what is being dried: concentrated sulphuric acid and phosphorus(V) oxide are acidic and must never be used with ammonia or other alkalis, while quicklime is basic and must not be used with acidic gases such as carbon dioxide, sulphur dioxide or hydrogen chloride. Calcium chloride is neutral and can dry most gases, but it cannot dry ammonia because it forms a compound with it.

items: Concentrated H2SO4: dries acidic and neutral gases; not ammonia or hydrogen chloride.
Phosphorus(V) oxide P2O5: powerful, acidic; not for ammonia.
Quicklime CaO: dries neutral and basic gases; not for acidic gases.
Anhydrous CaCl2: dries most neutral gases; not ammonia (CaCl2.8NH3 forms).
A drying tube or a wash bottle with the chosen desiccant is used in practice; the gas must pass through the agent slowly enough to be fully dried.

items.text: Drying carbon dioxide over quicklime would destroy the gas: CaO + CO2 -> CaCO3.
items.note: Choosing a drying agent by habit instead of by chemical nature is a classic exam error.

items.text: Drying ammonia with concentrated sulphuric acid fails: 2NH3 + H2SO4 -> (NH4)2SO4.
items.note: An acidic desiccant neutralises an alkaline gas — use quicklime for ammonia.

figures.caption: Figure: Choosing a drying agent safely
figures.description: Classify the substance first: acidic gas (use concentrated H2SO4 or P2O5, never quicklime), basic gas such as ammonia (use quicklime, never H2SO4 or CaCl2), neutral gas (anhydrous CaCl2 is convenient).

figures.caption: Figure: Removing hardness — decision route
figures.description: Temporary hardness (hydrogen carbonates): boiling removes it. Permanent hardness (sulphates/chlorides): use washing soda, ion exchange or distillation. Distillation alone gives completely soft, pure water.

keyPoints: A solution is homogeneous; a suspension settles; a colloid scatters light but does not settle.
A saturated solution holds the maximum solute at that temperature.
Water of crystallisation is fixed in number and is removed by heating, leaving the anhydrous solid.
White anhydrous copper(II) sulphate turning blue is the test for water.
Temporary hardness is caused by hydrogen carbonates and is removed by boiling.
Permanent hardness is caused by sulphates and chlorides and needs washing soda, ion exchange or distillation.
Hard water wastes soap by forming scum and forms scale in boilers.
The drying agent must not react with the substance being dried — match acidity to substance.
Distillation removes all dissolved solids and gives pure, soft water.
examFocus: Hardness questions usually ask for cause, example salt and removal method for each type — answer in that three-part form.
Drying-agent questions are trick questions: name the desiccant AND state why the wrong choices fail for that gas.
Water of crystallisation calculations use the mass lost on heating: mass of water = mass of hydrated crystal minus mass of anhydrous residue.
Percent-by-mass solutions use total solution mass as the denominator; percent-by-mass of an element uses the compound's Mr.

vocabulary.meaning: The substance dissolved in a solvent.
Solution holding the maximum dissolved solute at a given temperature.
Fixed number of water molecules in a crystal lattice.
Hardness removable by boiling, caused by hydrogen carbonates.
Hardness caused by sulphates/chlorides of Ca and Mg; not removed by boiling.
A drying agent that absorbs water without reacting with the substance.
Insoluble calcium/magnesium soap formed in hard water.

questions.prompt: Which substance would turn white anhydrous copper(II) sulphate blue?
questions.explanation: Water of hydration is added to the anhydrous salt to form blue CuSO4.5H2O; this colour change is the specific test for water.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing salt solution because it contains water — the test detects water molecules, but the standard reagent test is done with pure water; solutions give a weaker result.

questions.prompt: Hardness caused by dissolved calcium hydrogen carbonate is:
questions.explanation: Ca(HCO3)2 decomposes on heating to insoluble CaCO3, so boiling removes this hardness; the sulphates and chlorides that cause permanent hardness are unaffected.
questions.commonMistake: Confusing which removal method belongs to which cause; remember hydrogen carbonates decompose with heat.

questions.prompt: Which drying agent is suitable for drying ammonia gas?
questions.explanation: Ammonia is alkaline; it must be dried with a basic desiccant. Acidic agents neutralise it, and CaCl2 forms CaCl2.8NH3 with ammonia.
questions.commonMistake: Picking anhydrous CaCl2 because it is 'neutral and general' — it still reacts with ammonia specifically.

questions.prompt: The formula of blue vitriol is:
questions.explanation: Blue vitriol is copper(II) sulphate pentahydrate; CuSO4 alone is the white anhydrous form and FeSO4.7H2O is green vitriol.
questions.commonMistake: Confusing the number of water molecules; pentahydrate means five.

questions.prompt: Which observation shows that hard water is present?
options: Soap forms scum and little lather
questions.answer: Soap forms scum and little lather
questions.explanation: Calcium and magnesium ions react with soap to form an insoluble scum instead of lather — the standard field test for hardness.
questions.commonMistake: Linking hardness to boiling point or litmus, which reflect other properties entirely.

questions.prompt: Which method removes BOTH temporary and permanent hardness?
questions.explanation: Distillation boils the water and condenses the vapour, leaving all dissolved salts behind, so both types of hardness and every other dissolved solid are removed.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing washing soda — it softens both types effectively, but only distillation gives chemically pure water; where both are options, distillation is the complete removal.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: a mixture that settles on standing and scatters light is called a ________, whereas a ________ is homogeneous throughout.
questions.explanation: Suspension particles are large enough to settle under gravity; solution particles are molecular or ionic in size and never settle.
questions.commonMistake: Saying colloid — colloids scatter light but do not settle, which distinguishes them from suspensions.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: heating 25 g of CuSO4.5H2O (Mr = 250) leaves ________ g of anhydrous CuSO4 (Mr = 160).
questions.explanation: Mass of residue = 25 x (160/250) = 25 x 0.64 = 16 g; the remaining 9 g was water of crystallisation driven off.
questions.commonMistake: Subtracting 5 x 18 from 250 and then not scaling — always use the ratio of the anhydrous mass to the hydrated mass.

questions.prompt: Explain why pure water is called the universal solvent and state one limitation of this property.
questions.answer: Water dissolves a very wide range of ionic and polar substances because its polar molecules surround and stabilise ions and polar molecules, so more substances dissolve in water than in other common liquids. A limitation is that it also dissolves gases and minerals that can make water hard or unsafe, and non-polar substances such as oil and grease do not dissolve in it.
questions.explanation: The polarity that makes water a powerful solvent for salts is also why it picks up hardness minerals from rock and cannot dissolve non-polar oils.
questions.commonMistake: Describing 'universal solvent' without the polarity explanation, which is where the marks are.

questions.prompt: Distinguish between temporary and permanent hardness of water, giving the cause and one removal method of each.
questions.answer: Temporary hardness is caused by dissolved hydrogen carbonates of calcium and magnesium, such as Ca(HCO3)2; it is removed by boiling, which decomposes them to insoluble carbonates: Ca(HCO3)2 ->(heat) CaCO3 + H2O + CO2. Permanent hardness is caused by sulphates and chlorides such as CaSO4 and MgCl2; boiling does not affect them, so it is removed by adding washing soda, passing through an ion-exchange column, or distillation.
questions.explanation: The distinction rests on the thermal stability of the dissolved salts: hydrogen carbonates decompose on heating, sulphates and chlorides do not.
questions.commonMistake: Naming removal methods but not causes — most mark schemes award one mark each for cause and method.

questions.prompt: State what is observed when hydrated copper(II) sulphate is heated strongly and when the product is cooled and a few drops of water are added. Name the products in each case.
questions.answer: On strong heating, blue crystals turn into a white powder and colourless water vapour condenses on the cooler upper part of the test tube: CuSO4.5H2O ->(heat) CuSO4 + 5H2O. On cooling and adding water, the white powder turns blue again with a rise in temperature: CuSO4 + 5H2O -> CuSO4.5H2O.
questions.explanation: Heating removes water of crystallisation, giving the anhydrous salt; rehydration restores the hydrated form and is exothermic.
questions.commonMistake: Describing the white solid as a 'new compound' — it is the same compound without its water of crystallisation.

questions.prompt: A kettle scaled over with hard water is wasting fuel. Explain what the scale is, how it forms, and one way to prevent it.
questions.answer: Scale is mainly calcium carbonate (and calcium sulphate) deposited from hard water. When temporary-hard water is heated, calcium hydrogen carbonate decomposes to insoluble calcium carbonate, which sticks to the hot element: Ca(HCO3)2 ->(heat) CaCO3 + H2O + CO2. It can be prevented by using softened water (ion-exchange or distillation) or by removing the scale with a mild acid such as vinegar (ethanoic acid), which dissolves the carbonate.
questions.explanation: The insulating scale raises the energy needed to heat the water and can block pipes; prevention addresses the dissolved hydrogen carbonate before it deposits.
questions.commonMistake: Describing scale as 'dirt' or 'salt crystals' rather than the decomposition product of calcium hydrogen carbonate.

questions.prompt: A student needs to dry (a) ammonia and (b) carbon dioxide gas. For each, choose a suitable drying agent from quicklime and concentrated sulphuric acid, and explain why the other choice fails.
questions.answer: (a) Ammonia — dry over quicklime. Concentrated sulphuric acid would neutralise the ammonia (2NH3 + H2SO4 -> (NH4)2SO4), destroying the gas, and anhydrous calcium chloride forms an addition compound (CaCl2.8NH3), so neither can be used. (b) Carbon dioxide — dry with concentrated sulphuric acid. Quicklime would absorb the gas (CaO + CO2 -> CaCO3), removing the very substance being dried.
questions.explanation: A drying agent must not react with the substance being dried: match the acid-base character of the desiccant to the gas, and check for specific compound formation such as ammonia with calcium chloride.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing by habit rather than by reaction — the examiner looks for the failed alternatives and the reason each fails.

questions.prompt: Why does soap fail to clean clothes in hard water even though the water is otherwise pure and neutral?
questions.answer: Hard water contains dissolved calcium and magnesium ions. Soap is sodium stearate, and it reacts with these ions to form an insoluble calcium/magnesium stearate — the grey scum — instead of the soluble sodium stearate that would lower surface tension and form lather. The cleaning action depends on soluble soap molecules forming micelles around grease; once the soap is precipitated as scum, no cleaning occurs. The water's pH is unaffected, so the failure is chemical precipitation, not acidity.
questions.explanation: The question separates cleanliness from neutrality: neutralisation is not involved — a precipitation reaction removes the soap from solution before it can work.
questions.commonMistake: Blaming acidity or 'dirt in the water' instead of identifying the precipitation of calcium stearate.
